title: Score of Parentheses
description: Brute force to optimized: recursive substring parsing versus a single stack pass where each nesting level resolves and folds directly into its parent.

blocks.text: Given a balanced parentheses string s, return its SCORE according to these rules: "()" has score 1; "AB" (two balanced strings concatenated) has score A + B; and "(A)" (a balanced string wrapped in one more layer) has score 2 * A.

blocks.caption: A stack of partial scores, one per nesting level, directly implements the scoring rules: "()" contributes 1, and closing a wrapped level DOUBLES its contents' score before folding it into the parent

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Nested structure with rules that COMBINE based on depth (doubling per nesting level)","A stack, with each level of the stack representing the accumulated score of ONE nesting depth"],["\"AB\" scores as A + B (concatenation at the SAME level)","When a level completes, its score should be ADDED into its parent level's running total, not replace it"]]}

blocks.text: Each matched pair of parentheses either directly scores 1 (if it is an empty "()"), or DOUBLES whatever score its contents accumulated (if it wraps something nested inside); multiple such groups appearing side by side at the same level simply ADD their scores together.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Nested Bonus Multiplier System
blocks.text: Imagine a game where completing an empty task scores exactly 1 point, but completing a task that CONTAINS other sub-tasks DOUBLES whatever points those sub-tasks earned. Multiple sibling tasks (at the same level) simply add their points together. A stack, with one "current running total" per nesting level, directly tracks this: entering a nested task starts a fresh running total at zero, and completing it folds its (possibly doubled) score back into whatever level it was nested within.

blocks.caption: Each stack level accumulates its own score; closing a level resolves its value (1, or double if non-empty) and folds it into the parent level below

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Stack (top to bottom)","Why"],"rows":[["\"(\" : enter a new level","[0, 0]","A fresh nesting level begins, starting at 0"],["\"(\" : enter another new level","[0, 0, 0]","Nesting deeper"],["\")\" : close the innermost (empty) level: scores 1, folds into parent","[0, 1]","\"()\" directly scores 1"],["\"(\" : enter a new level","[0, 1, 0]","-"],["\"(\" : enter another new level","[0, 1, 0, 0]","-"],["\")\" : close the innermost (empty) level: scores 1, folds into parent","[0, 1, 1]","\"()\" scores 1 again"],["\")\" : close this level (value 1, non-empty): doubles to 2, folds into parent","[0, 3]","A wrapped, non-empty level always doubles"],["\")\" : close the outermost level (value 3): doubles to 6","[6]","The final wrap doubles everything accumulated inside it"]]}

blocks.text: Before building an explicit parse tree to represent the nested structure, notice that a stack, with each level tracking the accumulated score for its own nesting depth, directly implements the scoring rules in a single linear pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An opening parenthesis always begins a FRESH nesting level, which should start accumulating its own score from 0.

Observation 2: A closing parenthesis completes the CURRENT (innermost) level: if that level's accumulated score is still exactly 0 (meaning nothing was nested inside, an empty "()"), it resolves to a score of 1; otherwise, its accumulated score DOUBLES (the "(A)" rule).

Observation 3: Whatever score a level resolves to (1, or double its contents) must be ADDED into the PARENT level (the one just below it on the stack), correctly implementing the "AB = A + B" concatenation rule for siblings at the same depth.

Observation 4: A stack initialized with a single 0 (representing the "outermost" implicit level) elegantly handles the very top of the string uniformly, with the final answer simply being whatever remains at the bottom once the entire string has been processed.
This is a stack-based technique where each level accumulates its own score: closing a level resolves it (1 if empty, doubled otherwise) and folds that resolved value into its parent.
Recursively parse the string: split it into its top-level balanced pieces (siblings, summed), and for a string fully wrapped in one outer pair, recursively score its contents and double the result.

items: Determine whether the entire string is ONE single top-level group (fully wrapped in one outer parenthesis pair); if so, recursively score the inner contents and double the result.
Otherwise, split the string at every point the nesting depth returns to 0 (top-level sibling boundaries), recursively score each piece, and sum them.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Checking "is this the whole string one wrapped group" directly implements the "(A)" doubling rule.
Splitting at depth-0 points directly implements the "AB" concatenation (summing) rule for sibling groups.

blocks.text: Correctly computes the score, since it directly and recursively applies the exact rules given in the problem's definition.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case, since each recursive call may rescan a substring, and nesting can be up to O(n) deep.
Space: O(n), for the recursion stack and intermediate substrings.

Limitation: repeatedly re-parsing substrings (checking "is one group," splitting into pieces) is unnecessary overhead; a single stack pass computes the identical result directly, without ever creating substrings.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force repeatedly re-parses substrings recursively. Instead, use a single stack, where each level (from the moment it is entered via "(") accumulates its own running score. When a level closes (via ")"), resolve it (1 if it was empty, or double if it had accumulated some inner score), then IMMEDIATELY fold that resolved value into the new top of the stack (the parent level), continuing in a single linear pass.

Initialize a stack with a single 0. For each character: "(" pushes a fresh 0. ")" pops the current level's value v, computes its resolved score (1 if v == 0, else 2*v), and adds that resolved score directly to the new top of the stack. Return the final remaining value (stack[0]) after processing the entire string.
Use a stack where each nesting level accumulates its own score; closing a level resolves and folds it directly into its parent, all in one linear pass.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The remaining stack value is 3 (score of "()" is 1, plus score of "(())" is 2, totaling 3 via the "AB" concatenation rule).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case (deeply nested parentheses).

Each stack entry precisely represents "the accumulated score for whatever is currently open at this nesting depth." When a closing parenthesis resolves a level, the "1 if empty, else double" rule directly implements the problem's two base cases ("()" and "(A)"), and immediately folding that resolved value into the parent level directly implements the "AB = A + B" sibling-summing rule, since siblings at the SAME level naturally accumulate into the SAME stack entry as they are each closed in turn.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A level closes with accumulated value 0","It was an empty \"()\", resolving to exactly 1"],["A level closes with a non-zero accumulated value v","It had something nested inside, resolving to 2*v (the doubling rule)"],["Multiple sibling groups at the same level","Each one's resolved score is added into the SAME parent stack entry, naturally implementing summation"]]}

items: The initial stack seeded with a single 0 represents the "outermost" implicit level, letting the very first characters of the string be processed uniformly, without special-casing.
Resolving a level (1 or 2*v) and folding it into the parent happens in the SAME step, avoiding ever needing a separate "combine siblings" pass.
The final answer is simply whatever remains in the stack after the entire string is processed (which will always be a single value, since the string is guaranteed balanced).

blocks.text: When a nested structure's scoring rule DEPENDS on nesting depth (doubling per level, here), a stack where each level tracks its own running score, resolved and folded into its parent upon closing, directly and efficiently implements the rules in a single pass, without ever needing to build an explicit tree or re-parse substrings.

items: Forgetting to initialize the stack with a base 0 entry, which would require awkward special-casing for the very outermost level.
Resolving a closed level's score but forgetting to FOLD it into the parent (instead, say, storing it separately), breaking the sibling-summation rule.
Confusing "double the level's OWN value" (2*v, for a wrapped non-empty level) with "always contribute exactly 1," which only applies to a truly empty "()".

items: Explicitly stating "each stack level IS a running score, and closing a level always folds its resolved value into its parent" up front conveys the complete mental model in one sentence.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Nested scoring rule that DOUBLES per level, with siblings ADDING" points toward a stack where each level tracks its own accumulated score, resolved and folded into its parent on close.

items: How would the rule change if TRIPLING (not doubling) were used for wrapped groups instead? Simply change the "2 * v" resolution to "3 * v"; the rest of the technique applies identically.

How would you compute the MAXIMUM nesting depth simultaneously, in the same pass? Track the stack's size at each point, updating a running maximum, since stack size directly corresponds to nesting depth.

How does this connect to Remove Outermost Parentheses and Longest Valid Parentheses elsewhere in this category? All three rely on tracking NESTING DEPTH directly (via a counter or stack), rather than building an explicit parse tree, to solve structurally different but conceptually related problems.

The "each stack level accumulates its own score" technique, conceptually related to Remove Outermost Parentheses' depth-counter approach, both avoiding an explicit parse tree in favor of direct depth tracking.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (single stack pass, resolve-and-fold): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Stack where each nesting level accumulates its own running score

Core Idea: "(" starts a fresh level at 0; ")" resolves the level (1 if empty, else double) and folds that value directly into its parent level, naturally implementing both the doubling and sibling-summing rules in one pass
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Resolving and folding happen in the SAME step, letting siblings at the same level naturally accumulate into the same parent stack entry
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: "(" pushes 0; ")" pops v, adds (1 if v==0 else 2v) to the new top
